title: Biotechnology's third wave
titleCn: 生物技术第三次浪潮：酶与工业应用
articleHtml:
A 

For most of its history, biotechnology was associated with medicine and agriculture. A third wave, however, is now moving beyond hospitals and farms into factories, mines, paper mills and even clothing manufacturers.

 

B 

The central agents in this third wave are enzymes, natural proteins that speed up chemical reactions. The advantage is that enzymes are highly specific: a factory can achieve a desired result with fewer unwanted by-products than traditional chemical processes usually produce.

 

C 

Enzymes are not new to industry. By studying the structure of natural enzymes and altering the genes of microorganisms, scientists can produce enzymes that remain active in unusual conditions, such as extreme acidity or relatively low temperatures.

 

D 

One widely cited example is the textile industry. Some manufacturers of cotton fabrics now use enzymes to perform the same task more gently. The fabric becomes smoother and brighter, while less water and energy are consumed. For consumers, the final product may appear no different, but the method of production can be far less damaging.

 

E 

The paper and pulp industry has also experimented with enzyme-based processes. Conventional bleaching can involve chlorine compounds, which may produce harmful pollutants if not carefully controlled. Certain enzymes can help prepare the pulp for bleaching, reducing the amount of chlorine-based chemicals required.

 

F 

A further development combines enzymes with genetic engineering. Instead of simply finding useful enzymes in nature, researchers can insert selected genes into bacteria, yeasts or fungi, turning them into miniature factories. These organisms can then produce large quantities of enzymes for commercial use.

 

G 

The commercial appeal is obvious, factories may require less energy, produce less waste and rely less heavily on petroleum-based raw materials. However, critics warn that the environmental benefits are not automatic. Growing crops for bio-based products, for example, can compete with food production or lead to land-use problems if not managed carefully.

 

H 

Despite these concerns, many analysts believe the third wave could bring major environmental advantages. The promise is especially attractive because it links environmental protection with profit: companies save money while improving their public image.

 

I 

There remain obstacles. New biological processes must be reliable, safe and cost-effective before manufacturers will adopt them. Companies must prove that their methods do not create new risks. Nevertheless, the third wave of biotechnology is moving from the laboratory into everyday industry.
